Thank you all — I’m glad we’re here because too many families are one emergency away from financial ruin, and health care costs are crushing paychecks, savings, and peace of mind; that’s why our plan is practical, focused, and built to deliver real relief, not TV slogans. In plain English: we lower what people pay by tackling the biggest drivers of cost — prescription drugs, inefficient use of specialty care, surprise bills, and gaps in affordability — through a mix of concrete steps: negotiating lower drug prices and stopping abusive pricing practices; expanding access to primary and preventive care so people get care earlier and cheaper; banning surprise billing and making out-of-pocket costs predictable; and strengthening financial help so middle‑class families don’t face sudden premium spikes — and at every step we set measurable milestones, independent oversight, and public reporting so voters can see if the plan is working. We’re honest about the limits: some of the biggest savings depend on Congress and on careful implementation, which is why our rollout is phased — immediate regulatory and administrative actions where possible, paired with legislation for the broader changes — and why we’ve spelled out benchmarks and timelines in the policy brief. An independent fact‑check pushed back on the opponent’s “untested” attack and confirmed we’re drawing on proven tools and pilots; it also fairly noted that exact timelines and cumulative savings depend on legislative action and implementation choices — that’s a reasonable caveat, and it’s exactly why I’m asking voters to back a plan that pairs ambition with accountability. I’m running for the long, hard work of governing — to make health care affordable and reliable for families today and to make sure government actually delivers on that promise.

Q&A bullets for the candidate: Acknowledge the fact‑check’s nuance — “it pushed back on ‘untested’ and said our ideas have precedents, but noted savings hinge on Congress and implementation”; emphasize near‑term actions we can take administratively that start lowering costs right away; point to analogous state pilots and existing federal programs that inform our design when asked “untested?”; explain our phased timeline — immediate consumer protections and regulatory fixes, then larger legislative steps with clear benchmarks; highlight accountability — independent oversight, public reporting, and sunset/review clauses if targets aren’t met; pivot to contrast — ask the opponent to name specific policies and the math behind their ad’s claim.
